title: Krampus banned from Santa Claus parade, stirring controversy in Ontario town
summary: Krampus, a European Christmas folk creature, has been banned from Strathory, Ont.'s Santa Claus parade despite winning second place in the event's costume contest last year. Organizers say there were…

image.caption: Krampus is at the centre of controversy in Strathroy, Ont., after a tattoo and piercing shop was told it wasn’t allowed to show off the European Christmas character at the town’s upcoming Santa Claus parade. (Submitted by Tanya Griffin)

blocks.text: London

Krampus, a European Christmas folk creature, has been banned from Strathory, Ont.'s Santa Claus parade despite winning second place in the event's costume contest last year. Organizers say there were complaints that the figure wasn't family friendly.
A tattoo shop in Strathroy was told European folk creature isn't allowed at parade
Although he has a long, white beard and is dressed in a red velvet suit, his pointy horns and gaping snarl indicate that he certainly is not Santa Claus.

Krampus, a terrifying counterpart to Saint Nicholas, is the centre of controversy in Strathroy, Ont., after the half-goat, half-demon European Christmas character was banned from the town’s upcoming Santa Claus parade.

“Everyone had spent so much time on their costumes and they were really excited. Even the children were pumped to be a part of this float,” said Tanya Griffin, owner of Coven House, a Strathroy tattoo and piercing shop that entered Krampus in the parade.
“He was a celebrity. Everyone was cheering for Krampus,” she said of last year's float in the parade, where Krampus won second place in the costume contest.
The shop was told last week that Krampus wasn’t allowed back at the parade, which is set for this Saturday, Griffin said.

Tanya Griffin is owner of Coven House, a tattoo and piercing shop in Strathroy. An individual dressed as Krampus rode in Coven House’s Santa Claus parade float in 2025 and won second place in the parade's costume contest. (Jessica Singer/CBC)
The decision was made by the Strathroy Lions Club, which runs the annual parade, after the group received complaints that Krampus wasn’t family friendly, Griffin said.
CBC News has reached out to the local Lions Club but did not receive a response before publication.
Krampus is ‘demonic,’ church says
Krampus is a Christmas monster with roots in European folklore whose job is to reprimand children who have misbehaved, said Griffin.
“He’s basically the guy that takes care of the naughty list,” she said.
Krampus appears in popular parades and Christmas events in Germany and other nearby European countries. A Lions Club chapter in Austria also hosts a Krampus event.

Although Krampus is often depicted as an evil or menacing demon in books and movies, Griffin said her intention was never to scare children. She said she wanted to educate the community about European Christmas traditions and folklore.
Krampus in Strathroy's 2025 Santa Claus parade. The character rode in Coven House’s float and won second place in the parade’s costume contest. (Submitted by Tanya Griffin)
Children were going to dress up as woodland creatures and march alongside Krampus as part of Coven House’s float this year, handing out candy canes and temporary tattoos to spectators, said Griffin.
“I think the most shocking part about all of this is the inclusivity and the discrimination part of it.
“I feel like the Santa Claus parade should be about everything and everyone, and you shouldn’t be able to let one denomination, or one group, or one Krampus, out of it.”

items: Krampus, the European Christmas monster, is having a moment

blocks.text: CBC News obtained a letter written last year by the Calvary Church, a local Pentecostal church in Strathroy. Griffin said the letter was sent to the local Lions Club and delivered to her staff after last year’s parade.
In the letter, which is dated Dec. 10, 2025, the church writes that it was disappointed after satanic and demonic influences were promoted during the parade.
“Allowing the inclusion of satanic influences into what should have been a Christ-centred, Santa Claus Parade has caused a great displeasure,” the letter reads.
“To make matters worse, the parade judges awarded the float second place for costume and music, adding further insult as a result.”
The church was unable to provide an interview to CBC News, but suggested Googling Krampus to "read the article of what he stands for.... This will clarify our stand in the matter."
Brad Morrison, a minister at the Strathroy United Church, says religion shouldn’t dictate what can be displayed at local parades. (Jessica Singer/CBC)

Brad Morrison, a minister at the Strathroy United Church, said religion shouldn’t dictate what can be displayed at local parades. He said he dropped by the tattoo parlour after hearing Krampus wasn’t allowed in the parade to offer his support.
“There are other groups in town that are rather vulnerable, and if they’re targeted next, where does it stop?” said Morrison.
“I know that religion can be toxic. I know that people can use their religion as an excuse to exclude others. And part of my job is to stand against that.”
It’s important for communities to receive education about how different cultures choose to celebrate Christmas, Morrison said.
“Change in a small town is slow, but time’s on our side. We have a whole year of conversations about what are the values around cross-cultural understanding.”
The Santa Claus parade passes by Coven House on Frank Street, and on Saturday, Krampus will be standing outside her tattoo shop for spectators to see, Griffin said.
